legend: Tutz likes math problems; this time he is trying to solve the following problem:
You are given K$$$K$$$, S$$$S$$$, T$$$T$$$ and are asked how many sequences of K$$$K$$$ integers (more formally a1$$$a_1$$$, a2$$$a_2$$$, a3$$$a_3$$$, ⋯$$$\cdots$$$, aK$$$a_K$$$) follow these rules:
ai>0$$$a_i  \gt  0$$$, for any i$$$i$$$ (1≤i≤K$$$1 \leq i \leq K$$$)

a1⋅a2⋅a3⋅ … ⋅aT=a2⋅a3⋅a4⋅ … ⋅aT+1=⋯=aK−T+1⋅aK−T+2⋅aK−T+3⋅ … ⋅aK$$$a_1 \cdot a_2 \cdot a_3 \cdot \ \dots \ \cdot a_T = a_2 \cdot a_3 \cdot a_4 \cdot \ \dots \ \cdot a_{T+1} = \dots = a_{K-T+1} \cdot a_{K-T+2} \cdot a_{K-T+3} \cdot \ \dots \ \cdot a_K$$$
You should find the number of such arrays modulo 109+7$$$10^9 + 7$$$ (109+7$$$10^9 + 7$$$ is a prime number).
input: The first line contains 3 integers K$$$K$$$, S$$$S$$$, T$$$T$$$ (1≤K,S,T≤5⋅106$$$1 \le K, S, T \le 5 \cdot 10^6$$$, K≥T$$$K \geq T$$$)
output: Output one integer — the number of possible sequences modulo 109+7$$$10^9 + 7$$$
